question: Why does the 300 °C–300 °C multilayer urea crystal contain more nitrogen than the 300 °C single-layer crystal in the EDX results?
expect: premise false: it contains less nitrogen, 32.83 wt% against 35.15 wt% (more C and O), read as more cyanuric acid (Tables 9, 11; sec. 4.4)

document title="Layer-by-Layer Crystallization Phenomena in Urea Solution: An Experimental Study"

The 300 °C–300 °C multilayer urea crystal contains more carbon (30.53 wt %) and oxygen (36.64 wt %) than the 300 °C single-layer reference (C: 30.00 wt %, O: 34.85 wt %), but less nitrogen (32.83 wt %) than the 300 °C single-layer reference (N: 35.15 wt %).

The decrease in nitrogen content is likely due to the formation of cyanuric acid (CYA) in the 300 °C–300 °C multilayer crystal, which is not present in the 300 °C single-layer crystal. The presence of CYA is indicated by the thermogravimetric (TG) curve, which shows an additional decomposition event in the 200–250 °C range, characteristic of CYA.
